summary: A country occupying the whole Australian continent, where Aboriginal people have lived for more than sixty thousand years; British colonization began in 1788 and the federation was formed in 1901, and it is known for its diverse immigrant society and unique ecology.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: 'No religion' is Australia's fastest-growing category: in the 1966 census it was under 1 percent, and by 2021 it had risen to about 39 percent, becoming the largest single category. The spread of postwar education, urbanization, the social liberalization of the 1960s and 70s, and the church sexual abuse scandals since the 1990s (investigated by the Royal Commission of 2013-2017) have led many people to leave the churches, with an especially high share among the younger generation.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was first brought by the Irish convicts transported to New South Wales after 1788; Irish immigration continued to grow in the 19th century, and after World War II there were large numbers of Catholic immigrants from Italy, Malta, Croatia, Vietnam and the Philippines, so that in the 1980s Catholicism overtook Anglicanism as the largest denomination. The Catholic school system is huge, and about one fifth of students still attend Catholic schools.

ranking.name: Other Christians
ranking.description: Other Christians include Presbyterians, Methodists (who merged in 1977 with some Presbyterians and Congregationalists to form the Uniting Church in Australia), Orthodox Christians and Pentecostals. The Presbyterians were mostly brought by Scottish immigrants, while Orthodoxy arrived after World War II with Greek, Serbian and Russian immigrants, and Melbourne remains one of the cities with the largest Greek-descended population in the world.

ranking.name: Anglicanism
ranking.description: Anglicanism arrived with the First Fleet at Sydney in 1788 and was the de facto official church in the early colonial period; the first chaplain, Richard Johnson, came with the fleet. Because English immigrants long made up the majority, Anglicanism was the largest denomination, but with secularization and the diversification of immigrant origins its share has fallen from about four tenths in 1921 to about one tenth.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was brought to the interior in the late 19th century by the 'Afghan cameleers' (mostly from what are now Pakistan and Afghanistan), and the Marree Mosque in northern South Australia, built in 1861, is one of Australia's earliest mosques. After the White Australia policy was formally abolished in 1973, Muslim immigrants from Lebanon, Turkey, Bosnia and elsewhere increased, concentrated mainly in southwestern Sydney and northern Melbourne.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mostly skilled migrants and international students who have come since 2000 from India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Fiji. Because India has in recent years become one of Australia's largest sources of immigrants, Hinduism is one of the fastest-growing religions, concentrated mainly in Sydney and Melbourne.

religion.background: Before the arrival of Europeans, Aboriginal people had lived in Australia for more than fifty thousand years, and their beliefs centered on the 'Dreaming', which links ancestral spirits, the land and law. After British colonization in 1788, Christianity arrived with the colonists, and the sectarian rivalry between Anglicans and Irish Catholics affected education and politics in the 19th century. When the federation was formed in 1901, Section 116 of the constitution provided that the government may not establish a state religion. The postwar waves of immigration and the abolition of the White Australia policy in 1973 brought Orthodoxy, Islam, Buddhism and Hinduism, while secularization rapidly increased the non-religious population.

language.official: There is no statutory official language, and English is the de facto national language.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English arrived with British colonization in 1788; the convicts, free settlers and gold-rush population of the 19th century came mainly from Britain and Ireland, gradually forming a distinctive Australian English accent and slang (such as 'mate' and 'arvo'). Australia has no statutory official language, but English is the language of government, education and the media, and about 72 percent of the population speak only English at home, the rest being mostly from immigrant families.

ranking.name: Chinese (Mandarin)
ranking.description: The early Chinese speakers were Cantonese migrants of the 1850s gold rush, but from 1901 the White Australia policy long restricted Asian immigration. After the policy was abolished in 1973, immigrants and students from Taiwan, Malaysia and, after the 1990s, mainland China increased greatly, and Mandarin became the most commonly used non-English language in Australian households.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic speakers are mainly Lebanese immigrants who fled to Australia during the Lebanese Civil War of 1975-1990 and their descendants, along with refugees from Iraq, Syria and elsewhere. They are highly concentrated in areas such as Bankstown in southwestern Sydney, forming a sizable Arabic-speaking community.

ranking.name: Vietnamese
ranking.description: Most Vietnamese speakers are refugees ('boat people') from after the end of the Vietnam War in 1975 and their descendants; Australia was one of the first countries to accept Asian refugees on a large scale after the abolition of the White Australia policy. The Vietnamese community is concentrated in places such as Cabramatta in Sydney and Richmond and Springvale in Melbourne.

ranking.name: Cantonese
ranking.description: Cantonese is the oldest Chinese language in Australia: during the gold rush of the 1850s large numbers of Cantonese migrants from the Four Counties (Siyi) region came to Victoria and New South Wales. The wave of emigration before the handover of sovereignty over Hong Kong in the 1980s and 90s brought many more Cantonese speakers, but in recent years, with the increase of Mandarin-speaking immigrants, the share of Cantonese has declined relatively.

language.history: When Europeans arrived there were about 250 Aboriginal languages in Australia; after British colonization in 1788, because of the sharp decline in population, forced assimilation and the 'Stolen Generations' policies of 1910-1970s, most Aboriginal languages have disappeared or are endangered. English became the mainstream language of the colonies, and a distinctive accent developed in the 19th century. After the federation in 1901, the White Australia policy used a dictation test in English to restrict non-European immigrants, until it was formally abolished in 1973. Since then, multicultural policy has promoted community language education, and today more than 300 languages are used in Australian households.

ranking.name: Meat Pie
ranking.description: A palm-sized sealed pie, with ground beef and thick gravy inside a pastry crust, usually topped with tomato sauce; it is the most common takeaway food.
ranking.history: The meat pie came with British immigrants in the 19th century and was at first a convenient food for workers and gold miners to carry. From the 20th century the meat pie became the standard snack in the stands at Australian rules football matches, and brands such as 'Four'N Twenty', founded in 1947, made it popular across the country. It is often called Australia's 'national food', and in Adelaide there is also the 'pie floater', in which the pie is floated in pea soup.

ranking.name: Vegemite
ranking.description: A dark brown salty spread made from the yeast extract left over from beer brewing; its taste is strong and rich in B vitamins, and it is usually spread thinly on toast.
ranking.history: Vegemite was developed in 1922 by the Melbourne chemist Cyril Callister, commissioned by the Fred Walker company, using waste brewer's yeast from breweries. After World War I the import of Britain's Marmite was cut off, and Australia needed a local substitute. In the 1930s and 40s it was recommended by the medical community as a source of vitamin B and was supplied to the army in World War II, and it has since become a childhood memory and national symbol for Australians.

ranking.name: Pavlova
ranking.description: A meringue cake made by whipping egg whites and sugar and baking at a low temperature; the shell is crisp and the inside soft like marshmallow, and it is topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit.
ranking.history: The pavlova is named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, who toured Australia and New Zealand in 1926 and 1929. Australia and New Zealand have long argued over who invented the dessert: Australians say it was created in 1935 by Herbert Sachse, a chef at a hotel in Perth, but research shows that New Zealand recipes appeared earlier. Today it is the classic dessert on the Christmas table (which falls in the southern hemisphere summer) in both countries.

ranking.name: Lamington
ranking.description: Square sponge cakes are first dipped in chocolate sauce and then rolled in shredded coconut, sometimes split in the middle and filled with jam or cream; the texture is soft and sweet.
ranking.history: The lamington is generally thought to be named after Baron Lamington, Governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901, and the legend says his cook improvised it from leftover sponge cake, but its exact origin remains disputed. From the 20th century, schools and community groups often raised funds by selling lamingtons, called a 'Lamington Drive'. 21 July is designated National Lamington Day.

ranking.name: Anzac Biscuit
ranking.description: Sweet biscuits made from oats, shredded coconut, flour, butter and golden syrup, without eggs; the texture is both crisp and chewy, and they can be stored for a long time.
ranking.history: This biscuit is associated with the 'Anzac' (Australian and New Zealand Army Corps) of World War I: in 1915 Australian and New Zealand soldiers took part in the Gallipoli campaign, and women's groups at home made and sold biscuits to raise funds for the war. Because they contain no eggs and keep for a long time, they are often said to have been sent as comforts to soldiers at the front. Today every year on Anzac Day, 25 April, people make these biscuits to commemorate those who sacrificed their lives in the war, and the Australian government also requires that commercial products using the name 'Anzac' follow the traditional recipe.
